tanuki.origin: The raccoon dog, Nyctereutes procyonoides, is an East Asian canid, not a raccoon (Procyon); tanuki is its Japanese name, and in European fur farming it is known as Finnraccoon. Chinese geneticists describe the Chinese raccoon dog, N. p. procyonoides, as one of the most important fur-bearing species farmed in China, where it is raised alongside foxes and mink, for example in Hebei, Jilin and Xinjiang. Farmed stock includes the wild type and at least three coat color variants.
tanuki.structure: Raccoon dog pelts carry long, coarse guard hairs over a thick underfur, giving a shaggy, voluminous pile used mainly for trim. The hairs are keratin, with cuticle, cortex and a medulla in the guard hairs, and coat color depends on the amount and distribution of eumelanin and pheomelanin. Researchers ruled out alternative splicing and coding changes in the agouti signaling protein gene as the cause of the farmed color variants, so their genetic basis remains open. As with other furs, the skin must be dressed.
tanuki.process: Raccoon dogs are farmed in cages, pelted after the winter coat develops, and their skins dried, dressed and sometimes dyed before use as trim. Disease surveys report canine distemper virus, porcine circovirus 4 and Cryptosporidium in farmed raccoon dogs, reflecting the risks of dense and sometimes mixed-species husbandry; one porcine circovirus 4 detection came from a farm keeping pigs and raccoon dogs together. Experimental infection showed that raccoon dogs are susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 and transmit it to in-contact animals without showing illness.
tanuki.performance: The dense underfur and long guard hairs insulate well and give volume, but long hair tangles and breaks with abrasion, and dressed skins are sensitive to water and heat, so specialist cleaning is advised. Keratin hair is vulnerable to clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae in storage. In a laboratory study of pelts that included Finn raccoon, UV light failed to inactivate SARS-CoV-2, while heating at 60 C for one hour did.
tanuki.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) separate real hair from melting acrylic or modacrylic faux fur but cannot identify species. Because raccoon dog is easily confused by name with raccoon and by appearance with other long-haired furs, identification relies on guard hair microscopy against reference hairs and on DNA. Polymorphic microsatellite markers developed for the Chinese raccoon dog support individual identification and cross-amplify in Arctic and silver foxes.
tanuki.labeling: In the US, fur apparel falls under the Fur Products Labeling Act, whose FTC rules at 16 CFR Part 301 govern how the animal name and other information appear on labels, invoices and advertising. A trade name such as tanuki or Finnraccoon should not substitute for accurate species identification, and raccoon dog is not raccoon. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 requires textile products that contain non-textile parts of animal origin, such as fur trim, to state this on the label.
tanuki.past: Raccoon dogs are farmed for fur in Europe, where the Finnraccoon name is used, and in China, and the species became prominent in coronavirus research. Raccoon dogs were considered possible intermediate hosts of the SARS coronavirus in 2002 to 2004, and genetic analysis of environmental samples from the Huanan market in Wuhan found raccoon dog DNA in SARS-CoV-2-positive samples from a wildlife stall, placing the species on a shortlist of potential intermediate hosts. In 2025 EFSA identified locomotory disorders and isolation stress as species-specific welfare consequences for farmed raccoon dogs, alongside the movement and exploration limits shared by all caged fur species.

yangir.origin: Yangir is a rare trade term that this atlas links to ibex down. Its exact meaning could not be verified from primary sources: it may denote a species, a region or a brand. If ibex down is meant, candidate sources include the Siberian ibex, Capra sibirica, which genomic work shows has evolved superfine cashmere-type down, converging with the Tibetan antelope under cold plateau conditions. Wild Capra populations such as the Sindh ibex and markhor are used as wild references for the ancestry of domestic goats.
yangir.structure: Genuine ibex down would be expected to resemble cashmere. In double-coated species, a coarse outer coat covers a fine inner coat whose growth is seasonal, and in goats the fine down grows from secondary follicles. Comparative genomics points to extracellular matrix, focal adhesion and PI3K-Akt pathway genes, including type IV collagen and integrin families, as shared candidates for superfine down in Siberian ibex, Tibetan antelope and cashmere goats. Actual diameters, scale heights and medullation for any product sold as yangir should come from laboratory measurement, not marketing.
yangir.process: Down from a wild caprine could in principle be collected as shed fiber, combed from captured animals or recovered from hides of hunted animals; which route applies to yangir-labeled goods could not be verified. After collection it would need dehairing, scouring, carding and spinning as for cashmere. Because wild-animal collection raises questions of permits, hunting rules and species protection, a buyer or researcher should ask which species was sampled, where and how fiber was collected, who dehaired it, and which laboratory confirmed the species.
yangir.performance: No independent performance data for yangir were found. A fine caprine down would share cashmere's behavior: hygroscopic keratin, warm for its weight, self-extinguishing in flame, dyeable with acid dyes, prone to pilling and abrasion in lightly twisted yarns, liable to felt under heat, moisture and agitation, and attractive to clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae. Claims of superiority over cashmere should be treated as unverified marketing.
yangir.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) cannot identify the species. Microscopy can measure diameter and scale form but may not separate closely related Capra downs. Species confirmation would require DNA analysis or peptide mass spectrometry against authenticated ibex reference material; proteomic markers already distinguish cashmere, wool and yak, but validated ibex markers were not found in this review.
yangir.labeling: Yangir is not a generic fiber name in the US or the EU. Ibex is not among the specialty fibers of the US Wool Products Labeling Act, so under 16 CFR 303.6 the content would be disclosed with the animal's name and the word hair, fiber or blend when present at 5% or more, or as fur fiber. In the EU it would fall in the animal hair category of Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Trade in products of wild animals may also require CITES or national permits, depending on the species.
yangir.past: Independently verified history for the yangir name, including origin dates, producers or trade routes, was not found, and none is invented here. The broader context is the long human use of goat fibers: domestic goats descend from wild Capra populations, and breeds selected for cashmere carry genomic signatures of selection at hair-growth genes such as fibroblast growth factor 5. Rare-fiber names can circulate with little public documentation, which is why this atlas treats yangir as a research lead rather than an established material.
